claim: The Arabidopsis mutant wrky33 is highly susceptible to Botrytis cinerea.
source: The Arabidopsis mutant wrky33 is highly susceptible to Botrytis cinerea.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: More than 1680 Botrytis-induced WRKY33 binding sites associated with 1576 Arabidopsis genes were identified.
source: We identified >1680 Botrytis-induced WRKY33 binding sites associated with 1576 Arabidopsis genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 318 functional direct target genes of WRKY33 were defined at 14 hr post inoculation through transcriptional profiling.
source: Transcriptional profiling defined 318 functional direct target genes at 14 hr post inoculation.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: WRKY33 possesses dual functionality acting either as a repressor or as an activator in a promoter-context dependent manner.
source: Comparative analyses revealed that WRKY33 possesses dual functionality acting either as a repressor or as an activator in a promoter-context dependent manner.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparative analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing both activation and repression of target genes.

claim: Abscisic acid (ABA) plays a novel negative role in resistance towards B. cinerea 2100.
source: We confirmed known WRKY33 targets involved in hormone signaling and phytoalexin biosynthesis, but also uncovered a novel negative role of abscisic acid (ABA) in resistance towards B. cinerea 2100.
evidence: This is supported by genetic studies with ABA mutants and hormone measurements.

claim: NCED3 and NCED5 are direct targets of WRKY33 required for WRKY33-mediated resistance.
source: The ABA biosynthesis genes NCED3 and NCED5 were identified as direct targets required for WRKY33-mediated resistance.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq showing WRKY33 binding to these genes and genetic studies showing restoration of resistance in wrky33 nced3 nced5 triple mutants.

claim: Loss-of-WRKY33 function resulted in elevated ABA levels.
source: Loss-of-WRKY33 function resulted in elevated ABA levels and genetic studies confirmed that WRKY33 acts upstream of NCED3/NCED5 to negatively regulate ABA biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by phytohormone measurements showing increased ABA in wrky33 mutants.

claim: WRKY33 acts upstream of NCED3/NCED5 to negatively regulate ABA biosynthesis.
source: Loss-of-WRKY33 function resulted in elevated ABA levels and genetic studies confirmed that WRKY33 acts upstream of NCED3/NCED5 to negatively regulate ABA biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis studies and expression analysis.

claim: Necrotrophic fungi including Botrytis cinerea, Fusarium oxysporum, and Alternaria brassicicola are the largest class of fungal phytopathogens causing serious crop losses worldwide.
source: Necrotrophic fungi including Botrytis cinerea, Fusarium oxysporum, and Alternaria brassicicola are the largest class of fungal phytopathogens causing serious crop losses worldwide (Łaźniewska et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Necrotrophic pathogens extract nutrients from dead host cells by producing a variety of phytotoxic compounds and cell wall degrading enzymes.
source: These pathogens extract nutrients from dead host cells by producing a variety of phytotoxic compounds and cell wall degrading enzymes (Williamson et al., 2007; Mengiste, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: B. cinerea has a broad host-range and causes pre- and postharvest disease.
source: B. cinerea has a broad host-range, causes pre- and postharvest disease, and is the second most agriculturally important fungal plant pathogen (Dean et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: B. cinerea is the second most agriculturally important fungal plant pathogen.
source: B. cinerea has a broad host-range, causes pre- and postharvest disease, and is the second most agriculturally important fungal plant pathogen (Dean et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Plant immunity towards B. cinerea appears to be under complex poorly understood genetic control.
source: Plant immunity towards B. cinerea appears to be under complex poorly understood genetic control (Rowe and Kliebenstein, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Apart from the Arabidopsis thaliana RESISTANCE TO LEPTOSPHAERIA MACULANS 3 (RLM3), no major R-gene has been associated with resistance to necrotrophs.
source: Apart from the Arabidopsis thaliana RESISTANCE TO LEPTOSPHAERIA MACULANS 3 (RLM3), no major R-gene has been associated with resistance to necrotrophs.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Over the past two decades numerous genes that influence the outcome of B. cinerea—host interactions have been identified.
source: However, over the past two decades numerous genes that influence the outcome of B. cinerea—host interactions have been identified (Mengiste, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Several transcription factors are consistent with the large transcriptional reprogramming observed in host cells upon Botrytis infection.
source: Among these are several transcription factors (TFs) consistent with the large transcriptional reprogramming observed in host cells upon Botrytis infection (Birkenbihl and Somssich, 2011; Birkenbihl et al., 2012; Windram et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BOS1 (BOTRYTIS SUSCEPTIBLE 1)/MYB108 appears to restrict necrosis triggered by B. cinerea and A. brassicicola.
source: BOS1 (BOTRYTIS SUSCEPTIBLE 1)/MYB108 appears to restrict necrosis triggered by B. cinerea and A. brassicicola, and loss-of-BOS1 function increased plant susceptibility (Mengiste, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Loss-of-BOS1 function increased plant susceptibility to B. cinerea and A. brassicicola.
source: BOS1 (BOTRYTIS SUSCEPTIBLE 1)/MYB108 appears to restrict necrosis triggered by B. cinerea and A. brassicicola, and loss-of-BOS1 function increased plant susceptibility (Mengiste, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: BOS1 physically interacts with and is ubiquitinated by BOI, a RING E3 ligase that contributes to defense by restricting the extent of necrosis.
source: In response to stress and B. cinerea infection, BOS1 physically interacts with and is ubiquitinated by BOI, a RING E3 ligase that contributes to defense by restricting the extent of necrosis (Luo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MYB51 is involved in the transcriptional activation of indole glucosinolate biosynthetic genes, which contributes to resistance towards necrotrophs.
source: MYB51 is involved in the transcriptional activation of indole glucosinolate biosynthetic genes, which also contributes to resistance towards necrotrophs (Kliebenstein et al., 2005; Sánchez-Vallet et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The nac019 nac055 double mutant showed increased resistance to B. cinerea compared with WT plants.
source: In contrast, the nac019 nac055 double mutant showed increased resistance to B. cinerea compared with WT plants.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Ethylene and jasmonic acid (ET, JA) signaling are critical for host immunity to necrotrophic pathogens.
source: Ethylene and jasmonic acid (ET, JA) signaling are critical for host immunity to necrotrophic pathogens, and several transcriptional activators and repressors of the ET and JA pathways impact resistance to B. cinerea (Glazebrook, 2005; Bari and Jones, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Several transcriptional activators and repressors of the ET and JA pathways impact resistance to B. cinerea.
source: Ethylene and jasmonic acid (ET, JA) signaling are critical for host immunity to necrotrophic pathogens, and several transcriptional activators and repressors of the ET and JA pathways impact resistance to B. cinerea (Glazebrook, 2005; Bari and Jones, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The TFs ERF1, ORA59, ERF5, ERF6, and RAP2.2 have regulatory functions in host susceptibility to B. cinerea.
source: In particular the TFs ERF1, ORA59, ERF5, ERF6, and RAP2.2, have regulatory functions in host susceptibility to this fungus. (Berrocal-Lobo et al., 2002; Pré et al., 2008; Moffat et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Transgenic Arabidopsis lines overexpressing ERF1 or ORA59 confer resistance to B. cinerea.
source: Transgenic Arabidopsis lines overexpressing ERF1 or ORA59 confer resistance to B. cinerea (Kazan and Manners, 2013), whereas RNAi-ORA59 silenced lines were more susceptible (Berrocal-Lobo et al., 2002; Pré et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: RNAi-ORA59 silenced lines were more susceptible to B. cinerea.
source: Transgenic Arabidopsis lines overexpressing ERF1 or ORA59 confer resistance to B. cinerea (Kazan and Manners, 2013), whereas RNAi-ORA59 silenced lines were more susceptible (Berrocal-Lobo et al., 2002; Pré et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both ERF1 and ORA59 appear to be the key integrators of the ET- and JA-signaling pathways.
source: Both ERF1 and ORA59 appear to be the key integrators of the ET- and JA-signaling pathways (Pieterse et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The bHLH transcription factor MYC2/JIN1 is a master regulator of diverse JA-mediated responses by antagonistically regulating two distinct branches of the JA signaling pathway in response to necrotrophs.
source: In contrast, the bHLH transcription factor MYC2/JIN1 is a master regulator of diverse JA-mediated responses by antagonistically regulating two distinct branches of the JA signaling pathway in response to necrotrophs (Kazan and Manners, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The WRKY family of TFs modulates numerous host immune responses.
source: The WRKY family of TFs modulates numerous host immune responses (Pandey and Somssich, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: WRKY33 is a key positive regulator of host defense to both A. brassicicola and B. cinerea.
source: In particular, WRKY33 is a key positive regulator of host defense to both A. brassicicola and B. cinerea (Zheng et al., 2006; Birkenbihl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: WRKY33 was directly phosphorylated in vivo by the MAP kinases MPK3 and MPK6 upon B. cinerea infection.
source: WRKY33 was directly phosphorylated in vivo by the MAP kinases MPK3 and MPK6 upon B. cinerea infection and subsequently activated PAD3 expression by direct binding to its promoter (Mao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: WRKY33 activated PAD3 expression by direct binding to its promoter.
source: WRKY33 was directly phosphorylated in vivo by the MAP kinases MPK3 and MPK6 upon B. cinerea infection and subsequently activated PAD3 expression by direct binding to its promoter (Mao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: PAD3 encodes a key biosynthetic enzyme required for the production of the antimicrobial compound camalexin.
source: PAD3 encodes a key biosynthetic enzyme required for the production of the antimicrobial compound camalexin.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: WRKY33 directly interacted with its own promoter, suggesting a positive feedback regulatory loop on WRKY33 expression.
source: Moreover, WRKY33 directly interacted with its own promoter, suggesting a positive feedback regulatory loop on WRKY33 expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of WRKY33 binding to its own promoter.

claim: WRKY33 interacted with the VQ-motif containing protein MAP KINASE SUBSTRATE1 (MKS1/VQ21) and formed a ternary complex with the MAP kinase MPK4 within the nucleus of resting cells.
source: WRKY33 was also found to interact with the VQ-motif containing protein MAP KINASE SUBSTRATE1 (MKS1/VQ21) and to form a ternary complex with the MAP kinase MPK4 within the nucleus of resting cells (Andreasson et al., 2005; Qiu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Upon challenge with Pseudomonas syringae or flg22, activated MPK4 phosphorylates MKS1 thereby releasing WRKY33 from the complex and leading to its detection at the PAD3 promoter.
source: Upon challenge with the hemibiotrophic pathogen Pseudomonas syringae or upon elicitation by the microbe-associated molecular pattern (MAMP) flg22, the active epitope of the bacterial flagella, activated MPK4 phosphorylates MKS1 thereby releasing WRKY33 from the complex and leading to its detection at the PAD3 promoter.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Activation of Arabidopsis WRKY33 resulted in rapid and massive host transcriptional reprogramming upon infection with B. cinerea strain 2100.
source: We previously reported that activation of Arabidopsis WRKY33 resulted in rapid and massive host transcriptional reprogramming upon infection with B. cinerea strain 2100 (Birkenbihl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Susceptible wrky33 mutants displayed early inappropriate activation of salicylic acid (SA)-related host responses compared to resistant wild-type (WT) plants.
source: Compared to resistant wild-type (WT) plants, susceptible wrky33 mutants displayed early inappropriate activation of salicylic acid (SA)-related host responses, elevated SA and JA levels, and down-regulation of JA-associated responses at later infection stages.
evidence: This is based on prior experimental data from the authors' previous work.

claim: Susceptible wrky33 mutants had elevated SA and JA levels compared to resistant wild-type (WT) plants.
source: Compared to resistant wild-type (WT) plants, susceptible wrky33 mutants displayed early inappropriate activation of salicylic acid (SA)-related host responses, elevated SA and JA levels, and down-regulation of JA-associated responses at later infection stages.
evidence: This is based on prior experimental data from the authors' previous work.

claim: Susceptible wrky33 mutants showed down-regulation of JA-associated responses at later infection stages compared to resistant wild-type (WT) plants.
source: Compared to resistant wild-type (WT) plants, susceptible wrky33 mutants displayed early inappropriate activation of salicylic acid (SA)-related host responses, elevated SA and JA levels, and down-regulation of JA-associated responses at later infection stages.
evidence: This is based on prior experimental data from the authors' previous work.

claim: ChIP analysis demonstrated that WRKY33 directly binds to the regulatory regions of JAZ1 and JAZ5.
source: Consistent with these results ChIP analysis demonstrated that WRKY33 directly binds to the regulatory regions of JAZ1 and JAZ5, two genes encoding repressors of JA signaling, but also to the ERF class TF gene ORA59 involved in JA-ET crosstalk, and to two camalexin biosynthesis genes CYP71A13 and PAD3 (Birkenbihl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: JAZ1 and JAZ5 encode repressors of JA signaling.
source: Consistent with these results ChIP analysis demonstrated that WRKY33 directly binds to the regulatory regions of JAZ1 and JAZ5, two genes encoding repressors of JA signaling, but also to the ERF class TF gene ORA59 involved in JA-ET crosstalk, and to two camalexin biosynthesis genes CYP71A13 and PAD3 (Birkenbihl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: WRKY33 directly binds to the ERF class TF gene ORA59 involved in JA-ET crosstalk.
source: Consistent with these results ChIP analysis demonstrated that WRKY33 directly binds to the regulatory regions of JAZ1 and JAZ5, two genes encoding repressors of JA signaling, but also to the ERF class TF gene ORA59 involved in JA-ET crosstalk, and to two camalexin biosynthesis genes CYP71A13 and PAD3 (Birkenbihl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: WRKY33 directly binds to two camalexin biosynthesis genes CYP71A13 and PAD3.
source: Consistent with these results ChIP analysis demonstrated that WRKY33 directly binds to the regulatory regions of JAZ1 and JAZ5, two genes encoding repressors of JA signaling, but also to the ERF class TF gene ORA59 involved in JA-ET crosstalk, and to two camalexin biosynthesis genes CYP71A13 and PAD3 (Birkenbihl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: pad3 plants are susceptible to B. cinerea 2100.
source: Although pad3 plants are susceptible to B. cinerea 2100, wrky33 mutants are more highly susceptible.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: wrky33 mutants are more highly susceptible to B. cinerea 2100 than pad3 plants.
source: Although pad3 plants are susceptible to B. cinerea 2100, wrky33 mutants are more highly susceptible.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Altered SA responses at later infection stages may contribute to the susceptibility of wrky33 to B. cinerea, but were insufficient for WRKY33-mediated resistance.
source: Genetic studies revealed that altered SA responses at later infection stages may contribute to the susceptibility of wrky33 to B. cinerea, but were insufficient for WRKY33-mediated resistance (Birkenbihl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: WRKY33 apparently targets additional genes whose functions are critical for establishing full WRKY33-dependent resistance towards B. cinerea.
source: Thus, WRKY33 apparently targets additional genes whose functions are critical for establishing full WRKY33-dependent resistance towards this necrotroph.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that known targets are insufficient to explain full resistance.

claim: A transgenic wrky33 null mutant expressing an HA epitope-tagged WRKY33 construct under the control of its native promoter (PWRKY33:WRKY33-HA) complemented the B. cinerea 2100 susceptibility phenotype of wrky33 plants resulting in resistance similar to WT Col-0 plants.
source: For this, a transgenic wrky33 null mutant expressing an HA epitope-tagged WRKY33 construct under the control of its native promoter (PWRKY33:WRKY33-HA) was used. This line complemented the B. cinerea 2100 susceptibility phenotype of wrky33 plants resulting in resistance similar to WT Col-0 plants (Birkenbihl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: No WRKY33-HA protein was detected in the absence of infection.
source: No WRKY33-HA protein was detected in the absence of infection.
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 1684 high confidence WRKY33 binding sites common to both replicates were identified, which are associated with 1576 genes.
source: We identified 1684 high confidence WRKY33 binding sites common to both replicates, which are associated with 1576 genes (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: WRKY33 binding to all detected sites was dependent on prior infection with B. cinerea 2100.
source: WRKY33 binding to all detected sites was dependent on prior infection with B. cinerea 2100.
evidence: This is based on comparison of infected and mock-treated samples in ChIP-seq experiments.

claim: Over 78% of the identified peak regions were located in promoter (1 kb region upstream of the transcription start site) or 5′ intergenic regions.
source: Over 78% of the identified peak regions were located in promoter (1 kb region upstream of the transcription start site) or 5′ intergenic regions (Figure 1B) and 15.4% were located near transcription termination sites.
evidence: This is based on analysis of ChIP-seq peak locations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 15.4% of the identified peak regions were located near transcription termination sites.
source: Over 78% of the identified peak regions were located in promoter (1 kb region upstream of the transcription start site) or 5′ intergenic regions (Figure 1B) and 15.4% were located near transcription termination sites.
evidence: This is based on analysis of ChIP-seq peak locations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Less than 1% and 5% of the peaks were located in exons and intronic regions, respectively.
source: Less than 1% and 5% of the peaks were located in exons and intronic regions, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ChIP-seq peak locations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The genome-wide local distribution of peak regions relative to genes showed clear accumulation of WRKY33 binding at about −300 bp from the transcription start sites.
source: The genome-wide local distribution of peak regions relative to genes showed clear accumulation of WRKY33 binding at about −300 bp from the transcription start sites (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Nearly all previously reported WRKY33 in vivo targets including PAD3, CYP71A13, ACS2, JAZ1, ORA59, TRX-h5, and WRKY33 itself were successfully identified in the ChIP-seq dataset.
source: Moreover, nearly all previously reported WRKY33 in vivo targets including PAD3, CYP71A13, ACS2, JAZ1, ORA59, TRX-h5, and WRKY33 itself were successfully identified in our ChIP-seq dataset (Mao et al., 2011; Birkenbihl et al., 2012; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This validates the ChIP-seq data by confirming known targets from published literature.

claim: WRKY proteins specifically bind to a DNA motif, TTGACT/C, termed the W-box.
source: Numerous studies have revealed that WRKY proteins specifically bind to a DNA motif, TTGACT/C, termed the W-box (Rushton et al., 2010), although adjacent bases (W-box extended motifs) can also influence binding (Ciolkowski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Adjacent bases (W-box extended motifs) can influence WRKY binding.
source: Numerous studies have revealed that WRKY proteins specifically bind to a DNA motif, TTGACT/C, termed the W-box (Rushton et al., 2010), although adjacent bases (W-box extended motifs) can also influence binding (Ciolkowski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Of the 1684 identified WRKY33 binding regions, 80% contained the well-established W-box motif.
source: Of the 1684 identified WRKY33 binding regions, 80% contained the well-established W-box motif (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: W-box extended sequence motifs were found within the WRKY33 binding regions.
source: We also found W-box extended sequence motifs within the WRKY33 binding regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: The core sequence GACTTTT was reported to be bound by Arabidopsis WRKY70 and to be required for WRKY70-activated gene expression.
source: These W-box extended motifs also included the core sequence GACTTTT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), which was reported to be bound by Arabidopsis WRKY70 and to be required for WRKY70-activated gene expression (Machens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: One additional sequence motif, T/GTTGAAT, occurs in 60% of the WRKY33 binding regions.
source: Apart from the W-box and W-box variants, we found one additional sequence motif, T/GTTGAAT that occurs in 60% of the WRKY33 binding regions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: More than 48% (817 out of 1684) of WRKY33 binding peaks contained both the T/GTTGAAT motif and the W-box.
source: More than 48% (817 out of 1684) of WRKY33 binding peaks contained both this new motif and the W-box (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: WRKY33 does not bind to the T/GTTGAAT motif based on EMSA experiments.
source: A clear interaction (mobility shift) was observed between WRKY33 and the labeled W-box probe but not with W-boxmut and the two probes harboring the T/GTTGAAT motifs (M-3 and M-7; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on EMSA experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The functionality of the T/GTTGAAT motif remains unclear.
source: Thus, T/GTTGAAT does not appear to be a WRKY33 direct binding site and its functionality remains unclear.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EMSA results showing no direct binding.

claim: In WT plants, the expression of 6101 genes was altered twofold or more (p ≤ 0.05) compared to non-infected plants upon B. cinerea infection, with 3048 genes being up-regulated and 3053 genes being down-regulated.
source: In WT plants, the expression of 6101 genes was altered twofold or more (p ≤ 0.05) compared to non-infected plants, with 3048 genes being up-regulated and 3053 genes being down-regulated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In wrky33, upon infection, the expression of 7441 genes was altered more than twofold, 3583 of them being up-regulated and 3858 down-regulated.
source: In wrky33, upon infection, the expression of 7441 genes was altered more than twofold, 3583 of them being up-regulated and 3858 down-regulated.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: A common set of 4686 genes showed changes upon infection in both WT and wrky33 genotypes.
source: A common set of 4686 genes showed changes upon infection in both genotypes (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Comparative profiling of mock treated plants identified 705 genes that were differentially expressed between wrky33 and WT in the absence of the pathogen, 458 of them being up-regulated and 247 down-regulated.
source: Comparative profiling of mock treated plants identified 705 genes that were differentially expressed between wrky33 and WT in the absence of the pathogen, 458 of them being up-regulated and 247 down-regulated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Comparing the expression profiles of B. cinerea infected wrky33 and WT plants identified 2765 differentially expressed genes dependent on WRKY33, of which 1675 were up-regulated in the mutant (termed WRKY33-repressed genes) and 1090 were down-regulated in the mutant (termed WRKY33-induced genes).
source: Comparing the expression profiles of B. cinerea infected wrky33 and WT plants (wrky33 B.c vs WT B.c), we identified 2765 differentially expressed genes dependent on WRKY33, of which 1675 were up-regulated in the mutant (termed WRKY33-repressed genes) and 1090 were down-regulated in the mutant (termed WRKY33-induced genes; Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: Of the 318 WRKY33-regulated target genes, 240 (75%) were repressed upon infection while 78 (25%) were induced.
source: Of these, 240 (75%) were repressed upon infection while 78 (25%) were induced (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is based on combined ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: WRKY33 appears to have a prominent repressive role on the transcription of many specific host genes indicating a negative regulatory function of WRKY33 in mediating immunity to B. cinerea.
source: Based on this analysis, WRKY33 appears to have a prominent repressive role on the transcription of many specific host genes indicating a negative regulatory function of WRKY33 in mediating immunity to this pathogen.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that 75% of regulated targets are repressed.

claim: The overlap between observed WRKY33 binding and altered expression of the associated genes upon fungal infection was around 20% (318 of 1576).
source: The overlap between observed WRKY33 binding and altered expression of the associated genes upon fungal infection was around 20% (318 of 1576).
evidence: This is based on comparison of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: The fraction of overlap between TF binding and altered gene expression for WRKY33 is similar to values reported for other plant TFs such as EIN3, HBI1, and BES1.
source: This fraction is similar to values reported for other plant TFs such as EIN3, HBI1, and BES1 (Yu et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2013; Fan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Genes related to 'defense response' were highly overrepresented among WRKY33-repressed targets (38%) and in the WRKY33-repressed non-target sets (17%).
source: For example, genes related to 'defense response' were highly overrepresented among WRKY33-repressed targets (38%) and in the WRKY33-repressed non-target sets (17%), suggesting that WRKY33 mainly functions as a repressor of plant defense responses.
evidence: This is based on GO term enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: WRKY33 mainly functions as a repressor of plant defense responses.
source: For example, genes related to 'defense response' were highly overrepresented among WRKY33-repressed targets (38%) and in the WRKY33-repressed non-target sets (17%), suggesting that WRKY33 mainly functions as a repressor of plant defense responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high proportion of defense genes that are repressed by WRKY33.

claim: Nearly 18% of the WRKY33-induced targets were associated to defense responses compared to only 3% of the WRKY33-induced non-targets.
source: However, it is important to note that nearly 18% of the WRKY33-induced targets were associated to defense responses compared to only 3% of the WRKY33-induced non-targets.
evidence: This is based on GO term enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: WRKY33 can act as a direct activator of defense gene expression, very likely in a promoter-context dependent manner.
source: This indicates that WRKY33 can also act as a direct activator of defense gene expression, very likely in a promoter-context dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some defense genes are directly induced by WRKY33.

claim: Genes associated with responses to the phytohormone ethylene (ET; 21%) are particularly prominent among the WRKY33-induced targets.
source: Particularly prominent among the WRKY33-induced targets are genes associated with responses to the phytohormone ethylene (ET; 21%).
evidence: This is based on GO term enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: 42 out of 318 WRKY33-regulated targets are involved in cell death, and 38 of these appear to be repressed by WRKY33.
source: 42 out of 318 WRKY33-regulated targets are involved in cell death, and 38 of these appear to be repressed by WRKY33 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on GO term analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: WRKY33-mediated repression of cell death genes may be an important feature required to reinforce resistance towards the necrotroph B. cinerea that depends on dead host tissue to complete its life cycle.
source: This WRKY33-mediated repression may be an important feature required to reinforce resistance towards the necrotroph B. cinerea that depends on dead host tissue to complete its life cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biology of necrotrophic pathogens and the observation that WRKY33 represses cell death genes.

claim: 41 of the WRKY33-regulated target genes encode for various kinases, and the majority of these genes appear to be negatively regulated by WRKY33.
source: Furthermore, 41 of the WRKY33-regulated target genes encode for various kinases, and again the majority of these genes appear to be negatively regulated by WRKY33 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: LecRK VI.2 plays a critical role in resistance against hemibiotrophic P. syringae pv. tomato DC3000 and necrotrophic Pectobacterium carotovorum bacteria.
source: For the WRKY33-regulated target LecRK VI.2, a critical role in resistance against hemibiotrophic P. syringae pv. tomato DC3000 and necrotrophic Pectobacterium carotovorum bacteria has been demonstrated (Singh et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: WRKY33 binding was found at 133 TF gene loci.

claim: WRKY33 repression of the SA pathway is linked to modulation of host cell death responses.

claim: WRKY33 influences various hormonal responses upon infection with B. cinerea 2100.

claim: WRKY33 had both a positive and a negative functional relationship with a fraction of its direct targets.

claim: WRKY33 binds to the promoter region of NCED3 and to the 3′UTR region of NCED5.

claim: NCED3 and NCED5 are two major genes encoding 9-cis-epoxycarotenoid dioxygenase, a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of ABA.
source: Interestingly, our global binding studies also revealed that WRKY33 binds to the promoter region of NCED3 and to the 3′UTR region of NCED5 (Figure 4A,D), two major genes encoding 9-cis-epoxycarotenoid dioxygenase, a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of ABA (Leng et al., 2014).

claim: CYP707A3 is involved in ABA catabolism.

claim: CYP707A3 expression decreased in the wrky33 mutant and increased in WT plants after infection indicative of positive regulation by WRKY33.
source: WRKY33 also bound to the CYP707A3 promoter, a gene involved in ABA catabolism (Leng et al., 2014), but its expression decreased in the wrky33 mutant and increased in WT plants after infection indicative of positive regulation by WRKY33 (Figure 4G–I).

claim: WRKY33 represses ABA levels during B. cinerea 2100 infection, and this repressor function is an important component in host resistance to this pathogen.
source: These results suggest that WRKY33 represses ABA levels during B. cinerea 2100 infection, and that this repressor function is an important component in host resistance to this pathogen.

claim: aba2-12, aba3-1, and nced3 nced5 mutants accumulated much less ABA than WT plants.
source: Previous reports have shown that aba2-12 (Adie et al., 2007), aba3-1 (Léon-Kloosterziel et al., 1996), and nced3 nced5 (Frey et al., 2012) accumulated much less ABA than WT plants.

source: This clearly indicates that increased expression levels of NCED3 and NCED5 in the wrky33 mutant contribute to susceptibility toward B. cinerea 2100, and that a key function of WRKY33 in host immunity towards this pathogen is to repress ABA biosynthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic studies showing restoration of resistance in the triple mutant.

claim: A key function of WRKY33 in host immunity towards B. cinerea 2100 is to repress ABA biosynthesis.
source: This clearly indicates that increased expression levels of NCED3 and NCED5 in the wrky33 mutant contribute to susceptibility toward B. cinerea 2100, and that a key function of WRKY33 in host immunity towards this pathogen is to repress ABA biosynthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic studies showing restoration of resistance in the triple mutant.

claim: Application of ABA together with the fungal spore droplet to leaves of the wrky33 nced3 nced5 triple mutant partially rendered plants susceptible to B. cinerea 2100.

claim: CYP707A mutants affecting ABA metabolism were reported to accumulate more ABA than lines overexpressing ABA biosynthetic genes.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Resistance to the necrotrophic fungus Plectosphaerella cucumerina is negatively impacted by ABA, and wrky33-1 mutant plants exhibited an enhanced susceptible phenotype towards this pathogen.
source: Interestingly, resistance to the necrotrophic fungus Plectosphaerella cucumerina is also negatively impacted by ABA, and wrky33-1 mutant plants exhibited an enhanced susceptible phenotype towards this pathogen (Sánchez-Vallet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Stimulating NCED3 expression and ABA biosynthesis has been described as an important virulence strategy employed by the hemi-biotroph P. syringae DC3000 in Arabidopsis.
source: Stimulating NCED3 expression and ABA biosynthesis has also been described as an important virulence strategy employed by the hemi-biotroph P. syringae DC3000 in Arabidopsis (de Torres-Zabala et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Virulence of P. syringae DC3000 to Arabidopsis is strongly reduced in ABA mutants.
source: Virulence to this pathogen is strongly reduced in ABA mutants.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: The expression of several NAC TF genes associated with ABA regulation was affected upon Botrytis infection in a WRKY33-dependent manner.
source: In our experiments, the expression of several NAC TF genes associated with ABA regulation was affected upon Botrytis infection in a WRKY33-dependent manner.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data.

claim: Increased expression of NAC002 (ATAF1), NAC019, NAC055, NAC061, NAC068 (NTM1), and NAC090 was observed in the wrky33 mutant.
source: In particular, increased expression of NAC002 (ATAF1), NAC019, NAC055, NAC061, NAC068 (NTM1), and NAC090 was observed in the wrky33 mutant.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data.

claim: Transgenic Arabidopsis lines overexpressing NAC019 or NAC055 displayed enhanced susceptibility to B. cinerea.
source: Like ATAF1, transgenic Arabidopsis lines overexpressing NAC019 or NAC055 displayed enhanced susceptibility to B. cinerea (Bu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: ABA has been shown to induce NAC019 and NAC055 expression.
source: ABA has been shown to induce NAC019 and NAC055 expression (Jiang et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ABA can repress SA-, ET-, and JA/ET-dependent signaling but also positively affect some JA responses.
source: ABA can repress SA-, ET-, and JA/ET-dependent signaling but also positively affect some JA responses (Asselbergh et al., 2008; Ton et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Elevated ABA levels in the susceptible wrky33 mutant resulted in concomitant increases in SA, JA, and ACC levels upon B. cinerea 2100 infection, implying a positive effect of ABA on these hormone signaling components.
source: Our genetic and phytohormone studies showed that elevated ABA levels in the susceptible wrky33 mutant resulted in concomitant increases in SA, JA, and ACC levels upon B. cinerea 2100 infection, implying a positive effect of ABA on these hormone signaling components.
evidence: This is based on hormone measurements and genetic studies.

claim: Increased SA levels per se in the wrky33 mutant do not contribute to susceptibility as wrky33 sid2 double mutant plants are as susceptible to B. cinerea 2100 as the single mutant.
source: Increased SA levels per se in the wrky33 mutant however do not contribute to susceptibility as wrky33 sid2 double mutant plants are as susceptible to B. cinerea 2100 as the single mutant (Birkenbihl et al., 2012; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature and genetic data.

claim: Concurrent increases in ABA, JA/ET and SA have been observed in the interaction of Arabidopsis with P. syringae DC3000 and with the vascular oomycete pathogen Pythium irregular.
source: Interestingly, concurrent increases in ABA, JA/ET and SA have also been observed in the interaction of Arabidopsis with P. syringae DC3000 and with the vascular oomycete pathogen Pythium irregular (Adie et al., 2007; de Torres-Zabala et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the case of P. irregular, host resistance correlated with high ABA levels, whereas ABA mutants were more susceptible.
source: In the case of P. irregular, however, host resistance correlated with high ABA levels, whereas ABA mutants were clearly more susceptible.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Elevated ABA levels mainly activate NPR1-dependent SA signaling while not affecting the upstream EDS1-PAD4 pathway.
source: Our molecular analysis of Botrytis-challenged wrky33 and wrky33 nced3 nced5 plants confirmed that elevated ABA levels mainly activate NPR1-dependent SA signaling while not affecting the upstream EDS1-PAD4 pathway (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Increased ABA activated ACS2, ACS6, ERF1, and ORA59, targets involved in ET/JA signaling.
source: Increased ABA also activated ACS2, ACS6, ERF1, and ORA59, targets involved in ET/JA signaling.
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data.

claim: In the wrky33 nced3 nced5 mutant as in WT plants expression of ACS6, ORA59, ERF5 and PDF1.2 was significantly reduced.
source: In the wrky33 nced3 nced5 mutant as in WT plants expression of ACS6, ORA59, but also ERF5 and PDF1.2 (data not shown) was significantly reduced.
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data.

claim: Both wrky33 nced3 nced5 and WT genotypes are resistant to B. cinerea, indicating that ET/JA components ACS6, ORA59, ERF5 and PDF1.2 are not essential in maintaining plant resistance.
source: However, as both genotypes are resistant to B. cinerea these ET/JA components appear not to be essential in maintaining plant resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both genotypes are resistant despite reduced expression of these genes.

claim: The increased ABA levels in wrky33 during Botrytis infection may trigger the activation of currently unidentified downstream ABA-response factors that bind to ABA response elements (ABRE, ACGTGG/T) or G-boxes (CACGTG) present in some gene promoters, resulting in transcriptional activation.
source: It is conceivable that the increased ABA levels in wrky33 during Botrytis infection trigger the activation of currently unidentified downstream ABA-response factors that bind to the ABA response elements (ABRE, ACGTGG/T) or G-boxes (CACGTG) present in some gene promoters, resulting in transcriptional activation.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Several genes including NAC019, NAC061, FMO1, GH3.2, and GH3.3 contain conserved ABRE or G-box motifs, which could respond to and be activated by ABA.
source: Indeed, several genes including NAC019, NAC061, FMO1, GH3.2, and GH3.3 contain such conserved motifs, which could respond to and be activated by ABA.
evidence: This is speculation based on the presence of known ABA-responsive motifs in these genes.

claim: The elevated levels of SA in wrky33 during Botrytis infection may in part be responsible for the strong expression of the glutaredoxin gene GRX480/ROXY19 observed in this mutant.
source: In addition, the elevated levels of SA in wrky33 during Botrytis infection may in part be responsible for the strong expression of the glutaredoxin gene GRX480/ROXY19 observed in this mutant (RNA-seq data in this study; Birkenbihl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation based on the correlation between SA levels and GRX480 expression.

claim: GRX480 binds to class II TGA factors, thereby activating TGA-regulated SA responses while preventing their participation in JA-mediated signaling.
source: GRX480 binds to class II TGA factors, thereby activating TGA-regulated SA responses while preventing their participation in JA-mediated signaling (Zander et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Plants ectopically overexpressing GRX480 are susceptible to B. cinerea 2100.
source: Plants ectopically overexpressing GRX480 are susceptible to B. cinerea 2100 (Birkenbihl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In animals and humans, several TFs can act either as transcriptional activators or repressors, depending on DNA-binding sequences or interaction with additional co-factors.
source: In animals and humans, several TFs can act either as transcriptional activators or repressors, depending on DNA-binding sequences or interaction with additional co-factors (Alexandre and Vincent, 2003; Berger and Dubreucq, 2012; Sakabe et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Many human TFs function as repressors as often as they act as activators.
source: Moreover, many human TFs function as repressors as often as they act as activators (Cusanovich et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In plants, few factors with dual functions have been unequivocally characterized.
source: In plants, few factors with dual functions have been unequivocally characterized.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: In tomato, the transcriptional activator Pti4 can repress the expression of PR10-a by forming a complex with the SEBP repressor.
source: In tomato, the transcriptional activator Pti4 can repress the expression of PR10-a by forming a complex with the SEBP repressor (Gonzalez-Lamothe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In Arabidopsis, the TF WUSCHEL acts mainly as a repressor in stem cell regulation, but can function as an activator of AGAMOUS(AG) during floral patterning.
source: In Arabidopsis, the TF WUSCHEL acts mainly as a repressor in stem cell regulation, but can function as an activator of AGAMOUS(AG) during floral patterning (Ikeda et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: WRKY proteins can act as activators or repressors, and selected family members in diverse plant species have been identified as key regulators in diverse plant processes.
source: Also WRKY proteins can act as activators or repressors, and selected family members in diverse plant species have been identified as key regulators in diverse plant processes (Rushton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: WRKY53 can activate or repress the expression of genes, depending on the nature of the target promoter sequence.
source: WRKY53 can activate or repress the expression of genes, depending on the nature of the target promoter sequence (Miao et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: WRKY6 activates PR1 expression while suppressing the expression of its own gene, and that of its closely related family member WRKY42.
source: WRKY6 activates PR1 expression while suppressing the expression of its own gene, and that of its closely related family member WRKY42 (Robatzek and Somssich, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: WRKY33 is a bi-functional TF that can act as an activator or as a repressor in a promoter-context dependent manner.
source: Our data show that also WRKY33 is a bi-functional TF that can act as an activator or as a repressor in a promoter-context dependent manner (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8.

claim: WRKY33 positively regulates genes involved in camalexin biosynthesis such as CYP71A13 and PAD3 by directly binding to their promoter regions.
source: WRKY33 positively regulates genes involved in camalexin biosynthesis such as CYP71A13 and PAD3 by directly binding to their promoter regions (Mao et al., 2011; Birkenbihl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Two additional camalexin biosynthetic genes, AMT1 and CYP71A12, are positively and directly regulated by WRKY33.
source: Our study confirmed these observations and identified two additional camalexin biosynthetic genes, AMT1 and CYP71A12 that are positively and directly regulated by WRKY33 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutants of CYP71A13 and PAD3 are susceptible to the necrotrophs A. brassicicola and B. cinerea.
source: Mutants of CYP71A13 and PAD3 are susceptible to the necrotrophs A. brassicicola and B. cinerea (Zhou et al., 1999; Nafisi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Several Botrytis-induced ET response genes were targeted and positively regulated by WRKY33.
source: Beyond this, several Botrytis-induced ET response genes were targeted and positively regulated by WRKY33 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: WRKY33 had a negative regulatory relationship on the expression of >75% of all targets, implying that it mainly acts as a direct repressor of many defense genes following pathogen challenge.
source: Still, WRKY33 had a negative regulatory relationship on the expression of >75% of all targets, implying that it mainly acts as a direct repressor of many defense genes following pathogen challenge.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The simplest hypothesis for how WRKY33 exerts its dual regulatory functions is that WRKY33 is recruited to distinct repressor and activator complexes at defined promoter sites.
source: The simplest hypothesis would be that WRKY33 is recruited to distinct repressor and activator complexes at defined promoter sites.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Several WRKY33-interacting proteins containing a VQ motif have been discovered that influence defense gene expression.
source: For instance, several WRKY33-interacting proteins containing a VQ motif have been discovered that influence defense gene expression (Lai et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2012; Pecher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: VQ proteins appear to act as suppressors of defense-related genes via their interaction with WRKY factors.
source: VQ proteins appear to act as suppressors of defense-related genes via their interaction with WRKY factors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: The protein VQ4/MVQ1 appears to function as a negative regulator of WRKY-type transcriptional activators including WRKY33.
source: Indeed, the protein VQ4/MVQ1 appears to function as a negative regulator of WRKY-type transcriptional activators including WRKY33.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: In a transient Arabidopsis protoplast assay, stimulation by MAMPs resulted in degradation of VQ4/MVQ1 following MAPK-mediated phosphorylation enabling WRKY33 to activate transcription of a defense-related reporter gene.
source: In a transient Arabidopsis protoplast assay, stimulation by MAMPs resulted in degradation of VQ4/MVQ1 following MAPK-mediated phosphorylation enabling WRKY33 to activate transcription of a defense-related reporter gene (Pecher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Two proteins, SIB1 and SIB2, interact with WRKY33 via their VQ motifs.
source: Two other proteins, SIB1 and SIB2, have been reported to interact with WRKY33 via their VQ motifs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: The interaction between SIB1/SIB2 and WRKY33 was required to stimulate WRKY33 DNA-binding activity and very likely to positively regulate WRKY33-mediated resistance to necrotrophic fungi.
source: This interaction was required to stimulate WRKY33 DNA-binding activity and very likely to positively regulate WRKY33-mediated resistance to necrotrophic fungi (Lai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Four VQ protein genes (VQ8, VQ22/JAV1, VQ28, VQ33) are direct targets of WRKY33 and show altered expression upon Botrytis infection in wrky33 compared to WT.
source: Interestingly, four VQ protein genes (VQ8, VQ22/JAV1, VQ28, VQ33) are also direct targets of WRKY33 and show altered expression upon Botrytis infection in wrky33 compared to WT.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: VQ22/JAV1 functions as a negative regulator of JA-mediated defenses, and transgenic VQ22/JAV1 RNAi lines showed enhanced resistance to B. cinerea.
source: VQ22/JAV1 functions as a negative regulator of JA-mediated defenses, and transgenic VQ22/JAV1 RNAi lines showed enhanced resistance to B. cinerea (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Elevated levels of VQ proteins in wrky33 may contribute to the suppression of JA signaling and susceptibility to B. cinerea.
source: Thus, elevated levels of these VQ proteins in wrky33 may contribute to the suppression of JA signaling and susceptibility to this fungus.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known functions of VQ proteins and their altered expression in wrky33.

claim: Many members of the WRKY TF gene family, including WRKY33 itself, are targets of WRKY33.
source: Finally, many members of the WRKY TF gene family, including WRKY33 itself, are also targets of WRKY33.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data.

claim: The majority of WRKY genes are transcriptionally activated during immune signaling.
source: The majority of WRKY genes are transcriptionally activated during immune signaling (Pandey and Somssich, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: WRKY factors form a complex and highly interconnected regulatory sub-network that is positively and negatively affected by auto- and cross-regulation by various WRKY factors.
source: Experimental and bioinformatics analyses have revealed that WRKY factors form a complex and highly interconnected regulatory sub-network that is positively and negatively affected by auto- and cross-regulation by various WRKY factors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: The WRKY web appears to be deeply interconnected to various hormonal pathways at multiple levels, probably to ensure rapid and efficient signal amplification while allowing for tighter control in limiting the extent of the host immune response.
source: This WRKY web appears to be deeply interconnected to various hormonal pathways at multiple levels, probably to ensure rapid and efficient signal amplification while allowing for tighter control in limiting the extent of the host immune response (Eulgem, 2006; Llorca et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and represents an inference about the function of the WRKY network.

claim: Genome-wide binding analysis and transcriptional profiling have identified potential targets of WRKY33, a key transcription factor involved in mediating resistance towards the necrotroph B. cinerea 2100.
source: In summary, genome-wide binding analysis and transcriptional profiling have identified potential targets of WRKY33, a key transcription factor involved in mediating resistance towards the necrotroph B. cinerea 2100.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Genes involved in ABA biosynthesis and directly regulated by WRKY33 act at crucial nodes in the signaling cascade mediating resistance to B. cinerea 2100.
source: This study revealed that genes involved in ABA biosynthesis and directly regulated by WRKY33 act at crucial nodes in this signaling cascade.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined genetic, ChIP-seq, and expression data.

claim: Due to the complexity of the highly interconnected hormonal signaling networks targeted by WRKY33, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying resistance to B. cinerea 2100 remain to be fully elucidated.
source: Due to the complexity of the highly interconnected hormonal signaling networks targeted by WRKY33, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying this resistance remain to be fully elucidated.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitations of the current study and the need for further research.

claim: Global transcriptional profiling of infected wrky33 nced3 nced5 plants should prove extremely valuable to further narrow down key genes and sub-signaling pathways required to re-establish WT-like levels of resistance in this mutant.
source: In this respect, global transcriptional profiling of infected wrky33 nced3 nced5 plants should prove extremely valuable to further narrow down key genes and sub-signaling pathways required to re-establish WT-like levels of resistance in this mutant.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research based on the current findings.
